title: Volumes in Compose
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose and key terms of volumes in compose.
Choose and interpret a suitable Docker example connected to volumes in compose.
Predict an expected result and verify it using observable evidence in a controlled environment.

content.intro: This lesson covers Volumes in Compose. You will connect the named subtopics from the supplied Docker curriculum to a small, observable example. Work through the visual first, then use the example to form a prediction and check it against the actual behavior.
content.why_it_matters: Choose storage by lifecycle: named volumes are managed by Docker and are suited to persistent container data; bind mounts connect a host path to a container; tmpfs is temporary memory-backed storage on supported platforms. Verify data after replacing a container and practice restoration, not merely backup creation. Learning volumes in compose helps you make deployment behavior explicit and repeatable instead of relying on a command that happened to work on one machine.

items.title: Named volumes
items.text: A named volume is managed by Docker and can outlive a container; verify persistence by removing and recreating a disposable container while reusing the same volume.

items.title: Bind mounts
items.text: A bind mount exposes a host path inside the container. Check host path correctness, file permissions, and whether the container should have read-only access.

content_blocks.title: Guided walkthrough
content_blocks.text: Start with the supplied example for volumes in compose. Before running it, state what you expect to happen. Compare the real output with that prediction, then change one variable or setting in a disposable lab to test the boundary of the idea. If a command is not supported on your operating system or installed Docker version, consult the linked official reference and record the actual version rather than guessing.

content_blocks.title: Worked example: Volumes in Compose
content_blocks.code:
docker volume create codeleaf-data
docker run --rm --mount source=codeleaf-data,target=/data alpine:3.22 sh -c "echo saved > /data/check.txt && cat /data/check.txt"
docker run --rm --mount source=codeleaf-data,target=/data alpine:3.22 cat /data/check.txt
content_blocks.expected_output: Both runs print the saved value: the file is in the named volume, not only in the first container layer.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Run in a disposable local environment; verify the second run before removing the test volume.
content_blocks.reset_steps: After verifying persistence, remove only this test volume with `docker volume rm codeleaf-data` when no container uses it.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming that a successful start means the application is ready.
common_mistakes.why: A container can start while its dependent service is unavailable or the application is failing after startup.
common_mistakes.fix: Inspect health/status and logs; add a meaningful health check or retry strategy where appropriate.

common_mistakes.problem: Keeping required data only in the container writable layer.
common_mistakes.why: Replacing the container can discard that layer and its application state.
common_mistakes.fix: Select a named volume or an external storage system, then rehearse a restore.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying a command without checking context, target, or permissions.
common_mistakes.why: Docker commands affect the active endpoint and can change host resources or publish services.
common_mistakes.fix: Check `docker context show`, use an isolated lab, make the smallest change, and verify the resulting state.
